sections.title: Definition, pathogenesis and who gets it

blocks.text: Infective endocarditis (IE) is an **infection of the endocardial surface of the heart**. It usually involves a heart valve (native or prosthetic), but can also involve the lining of a chamber or great vessel, a congenital defect, or intracardiac foreign material such as pacing leads and surgical conduits. **Streptococci and staphylococci** cause most cases. Without treatment it is almost always fatal.

blocks.title: Acute vs subacute IE
rows: **Staph. aureus** (highly virulent); also Strep. pneumoniae, Strep. pyogenes
Fulminant; kills in under ~6 weeks if untreated
Insidious; course of well over 6 weeks
Severe febrile illness, changing murmurs, early emboli, rapid heart or renal failure
Fever, malaise, night sweats, weight loss, chronic stigmata (clubbing, splenomegaly)

blocks.title: Pathogenesis in four steps
items: **Endothelial damage**, classically from a high-velocity jet (VSD, mitral or aortic regurgitation)
A sterile **platelet–fibrin deposit** forms on the damaged surface
**Bacteraemia** (dental work, tooth-brushing, IV drug use, cannulae, skin sepsis, cardiac surgery, pacemakers) seeds the deposit
A **vegetation** of organisms, fibrin and platelets grows; the avascular valve and the fibrin mesh shield organisms from host defences, so prolonged bactericidal therapy is needed

blocks.title: Epidemiology (Davidson)
items: Incidence about **5–15 per 100 000 per year**; more than half of patients are **over 60**
Underlying lesion: rheumatic 24%, congenital 19%, other (calcified aortic valve, floppy mitral valve) 25%, **no known lesion 32%**
Case fatality about **20% even with treatment**, higher with prosthetic valves and resistant organisms

blocks.text: Risk follows the **jet, not the size of the lesion**: small high-pressure lesions (small VSD, PDA, MR, AR) are vulnerable, whereas a large low-pressure **ASD carries minimal risk**.

In the **elderly** IE is often non-specific (delirium, weight loss, weakness) and is easily missed. Enterococci (urinary source) and Strep. gallolyticus (colonic source) are common, and mortality is much higher.

The **aortic and mitral valves** are the usual targets; injection drug users are the exception. Predisposing substrates include rheumatic valve disease, congenital lesions (VSD, PDA, bicuspid aortic valve), degenerative disease (calcified aortic valve, floppy mitral valve with MR) and, at highest risk, **prosthetic valves and previous IE**.

blocks.title: Organisms: source and exam clue
rows: Classic **subacute** IE on a damaged valve
Skin sepsis, abscesses, IV and central lines, IV drug use
Now the **commonest cause of acute IE**; destroys valves, abscesses, normal valves
Linked to **colonic cancer**: colonoscopy is mandatory
Elderly patients; after GU disease or procedures
**Early prosthetic valve IE**; ~5% of native IE; Staph. lugdunensis is aggressive
Aortic valve, hepatosplenomegaly; serology; may need life-long antibiotics
Abscesses and emboli common; surgery often needed; high mortality

blocks.title: HACEK = slow-growing oral Gram-negatives
items: **H**aemophilus (now Aggregatibacter) aphrophilus
**A**ggregatibacter (Actinobacillus) actinomycetemcomitans
**C**ardiobacterium hominis
**E**ikenella corrodens
**K**ingella kingae

blocks.title: Microbiology by setting (Davidson Box 16.94, % of cases)
Prosthetic valve and culture-negative IE
items: **Early** prosthetic IE (first weeks after surgery; StepUp uses <60 days): mostly **coagulase-negative staph** introduced peri-operatively, often with a wound infection by the same organism
**Late** prosthetic IE behaves like native-valve IE (streptococci, staphylococci)
**Culture-negative IE (5–10%)**: usually prior antibiotics; otherwise fastidious organisms: **Coxiella, Bartonella, Chlamydia, Legionella** (and slow HACEK growth)

blocks.text: Strep. gallolyticus (Strep. bovis) IE = **look for colon cancer** (colonoscopy), even if the patient has no bowel symptoms.
Do not dismiss **coagulase-negative staphylococci** as skin contaminants when they grow in repeated cultures: they cause about 5% of native-valve IE and most early prosthetic IE.

"Most common organism" depends on the question. Local past papers key **viridans streptococci** as the commonest IE pathogen (classic subacute, dental source), but in Davidson's series **Staph. aureus** is the single commonest organism (38% of native-valve IE) and the commonest cause of **acute** IE. Read the stem: subacute/dental → viridans; acute, lines, IVDU → Staph. aureus.

Right-sided IE (mainly the **tricuspid valve**, less often the pulmonary valve) is the typical pattern in **people who inject drugs**. Staphylococcal tricuspid endocarditis is a common complication of IV drug use, and Staph. aureus can infect a previously normal valve.

blocks.title: Sources of right-heart bacteraemia
items: **Injection drug use**: non-sterile, shared equipment; contaminated lemon juice used to dissolve heroin (Candida); licking needles (mouth flora)
**Long-term central venous catheters** (parenteral nutrition, prolonged antibiotics) and **haemodialysis** access
**Pacemaker or ICD leads** and other intracardiac prosthetic material

blocks.title: Organisms in drug-injector IE
rows: **69%**: all the staphylococcal cases in Davidson's series; the commonest cause

blocks.title: Clues to right-sided IE
items: Tricuspid regurgitation: **giant systolic V waves** in the JVP and a regurgitant murmur at the left sternal edge
**Septic pulmonary emboli**: pleuritic pain, pleural rub, haemoptysis; CXR or CT shows **multiple cavitating lesions**
Pulmonary valve IE (occasionally, in drug injectors): early diastolic **Graham Steell** murmur at the upper left sternal edge

blocks.note: Look at: (A) a large vegetation on the tricuspid valve on echo; (C) CT chest with multiple cavitating septic emboli from Staph. aureus tricuspid IE.

blocks.text: **Staph. aureus bacteraemia** carries a 20–30% risk of IE (about 25% in Pocket Medicine). Every drug injector with Staph. aureus bacteraemia, emboli or a new murmur needs **echocardiography**.

Right-sided IE often does well: **uncomplicated** right-sided Staph. aureus IE may need only **2 weeks** of therapy, and a tricuspid valve damaged by IE usually does not need replacing if pulmonary artery pressure is normal.
The commonest organism in drug-injector IE is **Staphylococcus (aureus)**, not a streptococcus. This is a favourite past-paper MCQ.

KC Essentials says tricuspid regurgitation is rarely caused by IE (most TR is functional). Davidson lists **endocarditis in drug injectors** as a key **primary** cause of TR. Both are true: overall TR is mostly functional, but in a febrile drug injector new TR means IE until proved otherwise.

Suspect **subacute IE** when a patient with valvular or congenital heart disease develops **persistent fever, unusual tiredness, night sweats or weight loss**, or new valve dysfunction or heart failure. It may first appear as an **embolic stroke** or limb ischaemia. **Acute IE** is a severe febrile illness with prominent, changing murmurs and petechiae; chronic stigmata are absent and heart or renal failure develops quickly. **Post-operative IE** appears as unexplained fever after valve surgery.

blocks.title: Peripheral stigmata: tell them apart
rows: **Painful**, tender, raised nodules on finger or toe pulps
**Painless** flat haemorrhagic macules on palms and soles
Oval retinal haemorrhages with a **pale centre**

blocks.title: Raise the suspicion of IE when there is (Kumar)
items: A **new regurgitant murmur**
Embolic events or sepsis of unknown origin
Haematuria, glomerulonephritis or suspected renal infarction
Fever **plus** prosthetic material, IV drug use, a new conduction disturbance, a first episode of heart failure, typical blood-culture organisms, or Osler/Janeway/Roth lesions

blocks.title: Examination checklist
items: Heart: new or changing murmur, signs of failure
Hands: splinters, Osler's nodes, Janeway lesions, clubbing
Eyes: conjunctival petechiae; **dilated fundoscopy** for Roth spots
Teeth (source), spleen, urine dipstick
Spine tenderness (osteomyelitis/epidural abscess), hot joints, focal neurology
Line, pacemaker or ICD pocket sites

blocks.note: Look at: the whole-body map of IE signs with their frequencies (murmur, petechiae, splinters, Osler's nodes, Roth spots, splenomegaly, emboli).
Look at: clinical photographs of splinter haemorrhages, Janeway lesions, Osler nodes and Roth spots.

blocks.text: **Fever + murmur = exclude IE.** In a known rheumatic valve patient with fever, the differential is rheumatic activity, IE and chest infection; a **change in the murmur** favours IE.

Sterile vegetations can mimic IE: **marantic (non-bacterial thrombotic) endocarditis** in advanced cancer, and **Libman–Sacks endocarditis** in SLE (small warty vegetations on both surfaces of the leaflet). Both can embolise.

**O**sler = **O**uch (painful, immune). Janeway = painless (embolic). Source frequencies differ (Osler 5% in Davidson, 15% in Kumar): remember only that both are **uncommon but specific**, while a murmur is the commonest sign.
The two pillars are **blood cultures** (identify the organism and guide therapy) and **echocardiography** (vegetations, valve damage, abscess). Diagnosis is made with the **modified Duke criteria**.

blocks.title: Blood cultures: how to take them
items: **3–6 sets before any antibiotic**, without waiting for a fever spike
Separate **peripheral** venepunctures with strict asepsis, ideally hours apart (Davidson ≥6 h; at least ≥1 h in other sources)
**Aerobic and anaerobic** bottles; **never** from an in-dwelling line
The first two sets detect about **90%** of culture-positive cases
Repeat cultures during treatment to document clearance

blocks.title: Modified Duke criteria
rows: Typical organism (viridans strep, Strep. gallolyticus, Staph. aureus, enterococci, HACEK) in **two** separate cultures; or persistently positive cultures **>12 h apart**; or ≥3 positive over **>1 h**; or single Coxiella culture / phase I IgG titre >1:800
Echo shows a vegetation, an abscess or a newly dehiscing prosthesis; or **new valve regurgitation**

Predisposing heart lesion or **IV drug use**; fever **≥38°C**; **embolic** (vascular) phenomena; **immunological/vasculitic** phenomena (GN, Osler nodes, Roth spots, rheumatoid factor); cultures or echo suggestive but not meeting a major criterion
2 major, or 1 major + 3 minor, or 5 minor (or pathology of a vegetation)

blocks.title: Transthoracic vs transoesophageal echo
rows: Prosthetic valves, abscess, negative TTE with high suspicion

blocks.title: When to go on to TOE
items: TTE negative or non-diagnostic but **clinical suspicion high**
**Prosthetic valve**, cardiac device, previous IE or congenital heart disease
Suspected complication: new **AV block** or abscess
High-risk organisms: **Staph. aureus**, enterococci, fungi

blocks.title: Supporting tests
items: FBC: **normocytic normochromic anaemia**, leucocytosis; ESR raised; **CRP is better for monitoring**
Urine: proteinuria, **non-visible haematuria**; U&E (renal impairment)
Immunology: raised immunoglobulins, **low complement**, rheumatoid factor
ECG: **AV block** (aortic root abscess); occasionally infarction from coronary emboli
CXR: heart failure/cardiomegaly (left-sided); septic emboli or abscesses (right-sided)
Culture-negative: **serology** for Coxiella, Bartonella, Legionella, Chlamydia
Equivocal echo: cardiac CT (paravalvular abscess); **FDG PET/CT** (prosthetic valve or device); brain/spine imaging for emboli

blocks.text: A **negative echo does not exclude IE**; treat if suspicion is high. Equally, echo is **not a screening test** for fever alone or a single positive culture with low pre-test probability.

Echo sensitivities vary by source (TTE ~65% in Davidson's cardiology chapter, 50–90% in its infection chapter, 39–58% for native valves in Pocket Medicine; TOE >90% in all). For the exam: **TTE moderate, TOE >90%**.

blocks.title: Complications by mechanism
rows: Cusp perforation, chordal rupture → **acute AR or MR**, heart failure
Focal neurology, LUQ or loin pain
Brain, splenic, renal abscess; **vertebral osteomyelitis**, epidural abscess, septic arthritis

blocks.title: Fever still present after 48 h of correct antibiotics: think
items: **Perivalvular extension / abscess**
Drug reaction (fever settles once the drug is stopped)
Hospital-acquired infection: line site, urinary tract
Pulmonary embolism (septic in right-sided IE, or from immobility)

blocks.text: Prosthetic valve IE carries a particularly high morbidity and mortality: vegetations, thrombus or calcification can jam the occluder, and **dehiscence** produces a paraprosthetic leak. **TOE** is the investigation of choice.
New **AV block** in aortic valve IE = **aortic root abscess** until proved otherwise → TOE and a surgical opinion. Repeat ECGs during treatment to catch PR prolongation.
Complications (including emboli) can still occur **after antibiotics have started**. Glomerulonephritis is immune-mediated, so haematuria is common, but significant acute kidney injury is uncommon.

blocks.title: Principles
items: **Multidisciplinary team**: physician/cardiologist, cardiac surgeon, microbiologist
Blood cultures **before** antibiotics, but do not delay treatment in an unstable patient
**Prolonged IV bactericidal** therapy, usually **4–6 weeks**; combinations are synergistic
Remove the source: extract an abscessed tooth; remove infected lines, pacemakers or ICDs
Confirm a reported penicillin allergy is genuine before avoiding beta-lactams

blocks.title: Empirical therapy (Davidson, BSAC)
rows: Ideally **wait for cultures**; if needed, IV **amoxicillin ± gentamicin**

blocks.title: Directed therapy (Davidson Box 16.96)
rows: IV **flucloxacillin**; prosthetic: add gentamicin + oral rifampicin

blocks.title: Monitoring
items: Gentamicin: pre-dose **≤1 mg/L**, post-dose 3–5 mg/L
Vancomycin: pre-dose **15–20 mg/L**
Adjust to levels and renal function; follow **CRP** and fever for response (expect improvement within ~48 h)

blocks.title: A 2-week course (benzylpenicillin + gentamicin) is allowed for fully sensitive strep only if
items: Native valve and MIC ≤0.125 mg/L
No heart failure, aortic regurgitation or conduction defect
No thromboembolism and no vegetation >5 mm
Clinical response within 7 days

blocks.title: Indications for surgery (Davidson Box 16.98)
items: **Heart failure due to valve damage** (emergency if cardiogenic shock)
**Uncontrolled infection**: persistent bacteraemia/fever despite appropriate antibiotics (>5–7 days in US sources)
**Abscess** formation (often with heart block)
**Large left-sided vegetations** with high embolic risk (>10 mm in Pocket Medicine) or previous systemic emboli
**Prosthetic valve**, fungal, Staph. aureus or highly resistant organisms often need surgery
Start antibiotics **before** surgery

blocks.text: **Prevention.** Davidson: because prophylaxis has not been shown to work, **routine antibiotic prophylaxis is no longer offered**. The ESC (in Kumar) and US guidance still give it to the **highest-risk** patients (prosthetic valve or repair material, **previous IE**, unrepaired cyanotic congenital heart disease or palliative shunts) for **dental procedures that manipulate the gingiva or periapical region**, e.g. amoxicillin 2 g 30–60 min before. No prophylaxis for native MVP or MS, or for routine endoscopy or cystoscopy. For all patients with valve disease the ESC also advises regular dental check-ups and prompt treatment of any bacterial focus.

Guidelines differ. Empirical: Davidson uses vancomycin + gentamicin for acute IE; KC Essentials uses benzylpenicillin + gentamicin (vancomycin if staph suspected); Pocket Medicine (US) uses vancomycin + ceftriaxone. Duration: KC Essentials allows IV for 2 weeks then oral, whereas Davidson gives **4 weeks IV (native) or 6 weeks (prosthetic)**. Answer with Davidson.
Prophylaxis MCQs: if asked who would qualify, pick the **prosthetic valve / previous IE / cyanotic CHD** patient. Never pick native mitral valve prolapse, secundum ASD or a GI/GU procedure.

cards.back: Infection of the endocardial surface: a native or prosthetic valve, chamber or vessel lining, congenital defect or intracardiac device.

cards.front: Which septal defect carries minimal IE risk, and why?
cards.back: A large ASD: low-pressure flow does not damage the endothelium (unlike the high-velocity jet of a VSD).

cards.front: Case fatality of IE despite treatment?
cards.back: About 20%, higher with prosthetic valves and resistant organisms.

cards.front: Commonest cause of ACUTE infective endocarditis today?
Classic organism of subacute IE after dental work?
Strep. gallolyticus (Strep. bovis) endocarditis: which extra test?
cards.back: Colonoscopy, to look for colorectal cancer.

cards.front: Usual organism of early prosthetic valve IE?

cards.back: Coxiella burnetii, Bartonella, Chlamydia, Legionella (and slow-growing HACEK).

cards.front: Valve and organism typical of IE in drug injectors?
Risk of IE in Staph. aureus bacteraemia?

cards.back: Osler: painful finger-pulp nodules (immune). Janeway: painless palm/sole macules (embolic).
2 major, or 1 major + 3 minor, or 5 minor.
3–6 sets from separate peripheral sites, before antibiotics, not timed to fever, never from a line.

cards.front: TTE vs TOE sensitivity for vegetations (Davidson)?
New AV block during aortic valve IE suggests?
Davidson empirical regimen for acute IE?
cards.back: IV vancomycin + gentamicin (add oral rifampicin if a prosthetic valve).

cards.front: Name the five Davidson indications for surgery in IE.
cards.back: Heart failure from valve damage, uncontrolled infection, large left-sided vegetations, previous emboli, abscess.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old university student has an echocardiogram before joining a sports team. Several congenital and acquired lesions are discussed in the teaching session afterwards.
questions.leadIn: Which lesion carries the LOWEST risk of infective endocarditis?
questions.explanation: IE develops where a **high-velocity jet** damages the endothelium. A large ASD shunts at low pressure, so its IE risk is minimal, even though it is haemodynamically important.
whyNot: A small VSD produces a high-velocity jet: a classic IE site.
A PDA produces a high-pressure jet into the pulmonary artery and is a recognised IE site.
A bicuspid valve with AR is a recognised (moderate-risk) substrate.
Mitral regurgitation from a floppy valve is a common predisposing lesion.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man with aortic valve endocarditis asks why he needs weeks of intravenous antibiotics when his chest infection last year needed only 5 days of tablets.
questions.leadIn: Which feature of the vegetation best explains the need for prolonged bactericidal therapy?
options: Organisms sit in an avascular fibrin–platelet mass shielded from host defences
The endocardium has a barrier like the blood–brain barrier
Vegetations are composed mainly of neutrophils
questions.explanation: Valve tissue is **avascular**, and the fibrin–platelet mesh of the vegetation protects dense colonies of organisms from phagocytes. Long courses of high-dose bactericidal drugs (often synergistic combinations) are therefore needed.
whyNot: IE organisms are mainly extracellular within the vegetation.
Resistance varies by organism; many streptococci are fully penicillin-sensitive.
There is no such barrier; the issue is avascular tissue and fibrin protection.
Vegetations are mainly fibrin, platelets and organisms.

questions.stem: A 71-year-old man has had 2 months of fever and weight loss. His haemoglobin is low with a microcytic picture. Echo shows a vegetation on the aortic valve, and three blood culture sets grow Streptococcus gallolyticus.
questions.leadIn: Which further investigation is most important?
questions.explanation: Strep. gallolyticus (formerly Strep. bovis) bacteraemia is associated with **colorectal neoplasia**; the iron-deficiency picture is a second clue. Colonoscopy is mandatory.
whyNot: A dental source suggests viridans streptococci, not Strep. gallolyticus.
A urinary source is linked to enterococci.
The association is with the large bowel, not the upper GI tract.
Ultrasound cannot exclude a colonic tumour.

questions.stem: A 63-year-old woman had a mechanical mitral valve inserted 3 weeks ago. Her sternal wound has been red and discharging. She now has a fever of 38.6°C, and TOE shows a new paravalvular leak.
questions.leadIn: Which organism is most likely?
questions.explanation: IE in the **first weeks after valve surgery** is usually due to **coagulase-negative staphylococci** introduced peri-operatively, often with a wound infection by the same organism.
whyNot: Oral streptococci cause late prosthetic and native-valve IE, not early post-operative IE.
Enterococci come from bowel or urinary sources and are uncommon in early prosthetic IE.
Coxiella causes culture-negative aortic IE after contact with farm animals.
HACEK organisms are oropharyngeal and rare in early prosthetic IE.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old man who injects heroin has 10 days of fever, cough and haemoptysis. His JVP shows large systolic waves and there is a pansystolic murmur at the lower left sternal edge. CT chest shows multiple cavitating nodules.
questions.leadIn: Which structure is most likely infected?
questions.explanation: Large systolic V waves plus a regurgitant murmur at the lower left sternal edge mean **tricuspid regurgitation**. Cavitating lung nodules are **septic pulmonary emboli**. Together these point to tricuspid valve IE, typical of drug injectors.
whyNot: Pulmonary valve IE also sends emboli to the lungs, but gives an early diastolic (Graham Steell) murmur, not systolic V waves.
Mitral IE embolises to the systemic circulation, not the lungs.
Aortic IE embolises systemically and gives an early diastolic murmur.
Left-heart emboli would reach the brain, spleen and kidneys, not the lungs.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman who injects drugs is admitted with fever and a new tricuspid regurgitant murmur. Echo shows a tricuspid vegetation.
questions.leadIn: Which organism is most likely?
questions.explanation: In drug injectors **Staph. aureus** causes most IE (69% in Davidson's series) and typically attacks the **tricuspid valve**.
whyNot: Streptococci cause only ~8% of drug-injector IE.
Enterococci are uncommon (~2%) in drug injectors.
Candida occurs (e.g. contaminated lemon juice) but is rare (~2%).
Pseudomonas is characteristic but much less common than Staph. aureus.

questions.stem: A 46-year-old woman with rheumatic mitral regurgitation has had fever and malaise for 5 weeks. Over the past few days she has had small, raised, red, tender lumps on the pads of two fingers, each lasting a day or two.
questions.leadIn: What are these lesions?
questions.explanation: **Painful** raised nodules on the finger pulps are **Osler's nodes**, an immune-complex vasculitis of subacute IE. They are uncommon but specific.
whyNot: Janeway lesions are painless flat macules on the palms and soles.
Splinter haemorrhages are linear streaks under the nail, not tender pulp nodules.
Heberden's nodes are bony DIP swellings of osteoarthritis.
Nail-fold infarcts are small dark spots at the nail fold, not tender pulp nodules.

questions.stem: A teaching session reviews the physical signs found in a large series of patients with subacute infective endocarditis.
questions.leadIn: Which sign is found most often?
options: A new or changing heart murmur
questions.explanation: A **new or changing murmur** is present in about 90%. Splenomegaly occurs in 30–40%; clubbing (10%), Osler's nodes (5–15%) and Roth spots (<5%) are uncommon.
whyNot: Splenomegaly occurs in only 30–40%, mainly in long-standing IE.
Roth spots are rare (<5%).
Osler's nodes are uncommon (5–15%).
Clubbing is a late sign in about 10%.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old man with known rheumatic mitral regurgitation has a temperature of 38.4°C and tender nodules on two finger pulps. Two separate blood cultures grow viridans streptococci. TTE shows no vegetation.
questions.leadIn: How is this classified by the modified Duke criteria?
options: Definite only if a TOE shows a vegetation
questions.explanation: Major: typical organism in two cultures (1). Minor: predisposing lesion, fever ≥38°C and a vasculitic/immunological phenomenon (Osler's nodes) = 3. **1 major + 3 minor = definite.** Echo findings are not required when enough criteria are met.
whyNot: Possible needs only 1 major + 1 minor or 3 minor; this patient has more.
The criteria are clearly met.
A TOE is useful but not needed to reach definite here.
Echo evidence is only one of the major criteria and is not mandatory.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old woman with a 4-week history of fever and a known aortic regurgitant murmur is stable. IE is suspected.
questions.leadIn: Which blood-culture strategy is most appropriate?
options: Three or more sets from separate peripheral venepunctures before antibiotics
One set taken at the next temperature spike
Sets drawn through her existing central line
Start empirical antibiotics now and culture tomorrow
Aerobic bottles only, from a single venepuncture
questions.explanation: Take **3–6 sets** from separate peripheral sites **before antibiotics**, without waiting for fever spikes. Use both aerobic and anaerobic bottles, and never sample from an in-dwelling line.
whyNot: One set is too few, and cultures should not wait for a fever spike.
Lines give contaminated or misleading cultures and must not be used.
In a stable subacute patient, antibiotics should wait for cultures; prior antibiotics are the main cause of culture-negative IE.
Both aerobic and anaerobic bottles from separate sites are needed.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man is on day 5 of treatment for Staph. aureus endocarditis of the aortic valve. He has no chest pain. His PR interval has lengthened from 180 to 320 ms, and today he has 2:1 AV block. There are no ST-segment changes.
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation: Progressive PR prolongation leading to AV block in **aortic valve IE** means infection has spread into the **aortic root** near the conduction tissue. This needs urgent TOE and a surgical opinion.
whyNot: Gentamicin causes kidney and ear toxicity, not heart block.
Embolic MI is possible, but there is no pain and no ST change; progressive PR prolongation points to an abscess.
Hyperkalaemia gives peaked T waves and broad QRS; nothing suggests it here.
GN causes haematuria, not conduction disease.

questions.stem: A 47-year-old woman is in week 3 of treatment for mitral valve endocarditis. She suddenly develops a severe headache and drowsiness. CT shows an intracerebral haemorrhage in the territory of a distal middle cerebral artery branch.
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely underlying lesion?
questions.explanation: Infected emboli lodge in distal arterial walls and form **mycotic aneurysms**, which can rupture and bleed. Emboli and complications can occur even during antibiotic treatment.
whyNot: Hypertensive bleeds are deep (basal ganglia); nothing suggests hypertension here.
Berry aneurysms sit at the circle of Willis and cause subarachnoid bleeds.
Amyloid angiopathy affects the elderly with lobar bleeds; the IE context makes a mycotic aneurysm likelier.
Venous sinus thrombosis is not a typical IE complication.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man with diabetes and an infected foot ulcer is acutely unwell with a temperature of 39.6°C, BP 92/60 mmHg and a new early diastolic murmur. Blood cultures have just been taken. He has no drug allergies.
questions.leadIn: According to Davidson, which empirical regimen should be started?
questions.explanation: For an **acute** presentation (likely Staph. aureus from skin), Davidson advises empirical **vancomycin + gentamicin** with dose adjustment by levels. Amoxicillin ± gentamicin is for subacute presentations if empirical treatment cannot wait.
whyNot: Amoxicillin is the subacute empirical choice and does not cover staphylococci reliably.
Benzylpenicillin alone does not cover Staph. aureus.
Oral therapy is inappropriate in septic acute IE.
Metronidazole covers anaerobes only.

questions.stem: A 61-year-old man is being treated for native aortic valve endocarditis.
questions.leadIn: Which finding is a clear indication for cardiac surgery?
options: Pulmonary oedema from severe aortic regurgitation due to cusp perforation
A 3 mm mobile vegetation on the aortic valve
Fever settling by day 3 of antibiotics
questions.explanation: **Heart failure due to valve damage** is the leading indication for surgery. Others include uncontrolled infection, abscess, large left-sided vegetations with high embolic risk, and previous emboli.
whyNot: Small vegetations are not an indication; size matters (large, >10 mm in US sources).
A prompt response to antibiotics argues against surgery.
A sensitive organism is a good prognostic feature.
Haematuria reflects immune-complex GN, not a surgical indication.

questions.leadIn: Pick the single best option for each patient. Any option can fit one item, several items or none.

items.stem: A 34-year-old woman with known rheumatic mitral valve disease had a tooth extracted 6 weeks ago. Since then she has had low-grade evening fevers, night sweats and fatigue. She has splinter haemorrhages and a louder mitral murmur.
items.explanation: Step 1: insidious course on a **damaged valve** = subacute IE. Step 2: the portal of entry is the **mouth** (dental extraction). Oral commensal **viridans streptococci** are the classic cause.

items.stem: A 76-year-old man has lost 6 kg and has iron-deficiency anaemia with a positive faecal occult blood test. Echo shows an aortic vegetation and blood cultures grow a streptococcus.
items.explanation: Step 1: streptococcal IE with a **bowel source**. Step 2: iron deficiency plus occult blood points to a colonic lesion, and the streptococcus linked to colorectal cancer is **Strep. gallolyticus** (formerly Strep. bovis). Colonoscopy is mandatory.

items.stem: A 50-year-old woman receiving parenteral nutrition through a long-term central line after chemotherapy develops fever and a new murmur. Echo shows a large vegetation. Fundoscopy shows creamy-white fluffy retinal lesions.
items.explanation: Step 1: immunosuppression plus a long-term line (especially parenteral nutrition) is the setting for **fungal IE**. Step 2: fluffy white retinal lesions are **candidal** retinal lesions. Fungal IE causes abscesses and emboli, often needs surgery and carries a high mortality.

questions.stem: A cardiology clinic reviews five patients who are about to have a dental extraction involving manipulation of the gums.
questions.leadIn: Under ESC guidance, which patient would be offered antibiotic prophylaxis?
options: A 64-year-old with a mechanical aortic valve
A 30-year-old with mitral valve prolapse and mild MR
A 28-year-old with a secundum atrial septal defect
A 70-year-old who had coronary bypass grafting
questions.explanation: Step 1: Davidson notes that **routine** prophylaxis is no longer given because it has not been shown to work. Step 2: the ESC (quoted in Kumar) still covers the **highest-risk** groups (prosthetic valve or repair material, **previous IE**, unrepaired cyanotic congenital heart disease) for dental procedures that manipulate the gingiva. Step 3: only the mechanical valve patient fits. If given, amoxicillin 2 g is taken 30–60 min beforehand.
whyNot: Native mitral valve prolapse is not a highest-risk lesion.
A secundum ASD is a low-risk lesion.
Coronary bypass grafting does not involve the valves.
HCM is a moderate-risk substrate, not a highest-risk one.

questions.leadIn: Pick the single best option for each patient. Any option can fit one item, several items or none.
options: Giant systolic V waves in the JVP
Early diastolic murmur, left sternal border

items.stem: A 39-year-old man with aortic valve IE has flat, painless, red-brown spots on both palms and the soles of his feet that blanch poorly.
items.explanation: Painless haemorrhagic macules on the **palms and soles** are **Janeway lesions**, caused by septic micro-emboli. Osler's nodes, by contrast, are painful pulp nodules.

items.stem: Dilated fundoscopy in a 55-year-old woman with subacute IE shows oval haemorrhages, each with a pale centre.
items.explanation: **Roth spots** are retinal haemorrhages with a pale centre (immune vasculitis). They are rare (<5%) but classic.

items.stem: A 62-year-old man with fever and a mitral murmur has no rash. Which bedside finding is present in roughly two-thirds of IE patients, and reflects immune-complex glomerulonephritis or renal emboli?
items.explanation: **Non-visible haematuria** is found in 60–70%. Haematuria in a cardiac patient should prompt you to consider IE.

items.stem: A 27-year-old who injects drugs has fever, pleuritic chest pain and a tricuspid vegetation. Which neck finding would you expect?
items.explanation: Two steps: tricuspid IE destroys the valve → **tricuspid regurgitation** → the regurgitant jet produces **giant systolic V waves** in the JVP.

questions.leadIn: Pick the single best option for each patient. Any option can fit one item, several items or none.
options: Three or more peripheral blood culture sets

items.stem: A 68-year-old with a mechanical aortic valve has Staph. aureus in four blood culture sets. TTE is limited by acoustic shadowing from the prosthesis and shows no vegetation.
items.explanation: With a **prosthetic valve**, Staph. aureus and a non-diagnostic TTE, the next test is **TOE**, which sees 1–1.5 mm vegetations and abscesses (>90% sensitive).

items.stem: A 54-year-old is on day 4 of treatment for aortic valve IE. Which simple bedside test should be repeated to catch the earliest sign of infection spreading into the conduction tissue?
items.explanation: An aortic root abscess shows first as **PR prolongation, then AV block**, so **serial ECGs** are needed.

items.stem: A 49-year-old sheep farmer has an aortic valve vegetation, hepatosplenomegaly and three negative blood culture sets, with no antibiotics given.
items.explanation: Culture-negative aortic IE after **farm-animal contact** with hepatosplenomegaly suggests **Q fever** (Coxiella burnetii). The diagnosis is made by **phase I IgG serology**, which is a major Duke criterion.

items.stem: A 58-year-old is in week 2 of treatment for streptococcal IE. Which blood test is the better guide to her response to treatment?
items.explanation: Davidson: **CRP** is more reliable than ESR for monitoring the response to therapy.

questions.leadIn: Pick the single best option for each patient. Any option can fit one item, several items or none.
options: Acute aortic regurgitation from cusp perforation

items.stem: A 31-year-old who injects heroin has tricuspid IE. He develops haemoptysis and pleuritic pain. CT shows multiple peripheral nodules, several of them cavitating.
items.explanation: Right-sided vegetations embolise to the **lungs**, causing **septic pulmonary emboli** with cavitation and haemoptysis.

items.stem: A 57-year-old woman with mitral valve IE develops sudden sharp left upper quadrant pain with tenderness under the left costal margin.
items.explanation: Sudden LUQ pain in left-sided IE suggests **splenic infarction** from a systemic embolus.

items.stem: A 66-year-old man in week 2 of treatment for Staph. aureus IE develops severe low back pain, marked spinal point tenderness and new weakness of both legs.
items.explanation: Staph. aureus seeds bone: **vertebral osteomyelitis with an epidural abscess** compressing the cord.

items.stem: A 70-year-old with a mechanical mitral valve has IE. TOE shows a new jet of regurgitation outside the sewing ring and abnormal rocking of the prosthesis.
items.explanation: Two steps: a jet **outside** the ring is a paravalvular leak, and a rocking prosthesis means the ring is coming loose. Together these indicate **dehiscence**.

items.stem: A 44-year-old man with aortic valve IE suddenly becomes very breathless with pulmonary oedema. A new early diastolic murmur is heard.
items.explanation: Sudden heart failure with an early diastolic murmur in aortic IE = **acute AR** from cusp perforation. Heart failure from valve damage is an indication for surgery.

questions.theme: Antimicrobial regimens in infective endocarditis (Davidson / BSAC)
questions.leadIn: Pick the single best option for each patient. Any option can fit one item, several items or none.
options: IV benzylpenicillin plus gentamicin for 2 weeks
IV flucloxacillin plus gentamicin and oral rifampicin for 6 weeks
IV vancomycin plus oral rifampicin for 4 weeks
IV vancomycin plus gentamicin plus oral rifampicin (empirical)
IV amoxicillin with or without gentamicin (empirical)

items.stem: A 48-year-old man has native mitral valve IE. Cultures grow meticillin-sensitive Staph. aureus. He has no allergies.
items.explanation: MSSA on a **native valve**: IV **flucloxacillin for 4 weeks**.

items.stem: A 72-year-old woman with a bioprosthetic aortic valve has IE due to meticillin-sensitive Staph. aureus.
items.explanation: For a **prosthetic valve** with MSSA, add gentamicin and oral rifampicin and extend to **6 weeks**.

items.stem: A 69-year-old man has native aortic valve IE after a urological procedure. Cultures grow amoxicillin-sensitive Enterococcus faecalis.
items.explanation: Enterococci need **synergistic amoxicillin + gentamicin** (4 weeks native, 6 weeks prosthetic).

items.stem: A 66-year-old with a mechanical mitral valve is acutely febrile with a new paravalvular leak. Blood cultures have just been taken.
items.explanation: Two steps: the organism is unknown (empirical), and a **prosthetic valve** is suspected. Davidson: vancomycin + gentamicin **plus oral rifampicin**.

items.stem: A 58-year-old woman with a mechanical aortic valve has IE due to viridans streptococci with a penicillin MIC of 0.06 mg/L.
items.explanation: A fully sensitive streptococcus (MIC ≤0.125) is treated with benzylpenicillin, but a **prosthetic** valve needs **6 weeks**. The 2-week short course applies to native valves only.

questions.stem: A 41-year-old man has native mitral valve IE due to Strep. mitis (penicillin MIC 0.03 mg/L). He has no heart failure, no AR and a normal ECG. He was afebrile by day 4. TOE shows an 8 mm vegetation.
questions.leadIn: Which feature rules out a 2-week short-course regimen?
questions.explanation: The short course (benzylpenicillin + gentamicin for 2 weeks) requires a native valve, MIC ≤0.125, no HF/AR/conduction defect, no emboli, **no vegetation >5 mm** and a response within 7 days. The 8 mm vegetation excludes him.
whyNot: A native valve is a requirement for the short course, not a barrier.
An MIC ≤0.125 mg/L is required and is met.
A response within 7 days is required and is met.
A normal ECG (no conduction defect) is required and is met.

questions.theme: Fever, murmur or vegetation: most likely diagnosis
questions.leadIn: Pick the single best option for each patient. Any option can fit one item, several items or none.

items.stem: A 66-year-old woman with metastatic pancreatic cancer has an embolic stroke. TOE shows small mitral vegetations. Repeated blood cultures, taken before any antibiotics, are sterile and she has no fever.
items.explanation: Sterile fibrin–platelet vegetations in **advanced cancer** that embolise = **marantic (non-bacterial thrombotic) endocarditis**.

items.stem: A 28-year-old woman with a malar rash, arthralgia and positive anti-dsDNA has small warty vegetations on both surfaces of the mitral leaflets. Blood cultures are negative.
items.explanation: Sterile verrucous vegetations on **both sides** of the leaflet in **SLE** = **Libman–Sacks endocarditis**.

items.stem: A 42-year-old man had an aortic valve replacement 2 weeks ago. He now has a fever and an inflamed sternal wound, and 3 of 3 blood culture sets grow coagulase-negative staphylococci.
items.explanation: IE within the **first weeks** of surgery, caused by coagulase-negative staph from the wound = **early prosthetic valve endocarditis**. The cultures should not be dismissed as contaminants.

questions.stem: A 53-year-old dairy farmer has 4 months of malaise, sweats and weight loss. He has an aortic regurgitant murmur and a large liver and spleen. Three blood culture sets, taken before any antibiotic, remain negative.
questions.leadIn: Which organism is most likely?
questions.explanation: Culture-negative IE of the **aortic valve** with **farm-animal contact** and **hepatosplenomegaly** suggests **Q fever** (Coxiella burnetii). Diagnose by phase I IgG serology; life-long antibiotics may be needed.
whyNot: Staph. aureus grows readily in culture and causes an acute picture.
Viridans streptococci grow readily unless antibiotics were given.
Enterococci grow readily and come from bowel or urinary sources.
Coagulase-negative staph grow readily and usually involve prosthetic material.

questions.theme: Next step in managing infective endocarditis
questions.leadIn: Pick the single best option for each patient. Any option can fit one item, several items or none.
options: Remove the infected device or line
Check gentamicin levels and renal function

items.stem: A 59-year-old with native aortic valve IE develops acute pulmonary oedema with free aortic regurgitation on echo, despite 4 days of appropriate antibiotics.
items.explanation: **Heart failure due to valve destruction** is the leading indication for surgery. Antibiotics continue, but the valve must be replaced.

items.stem: A 72-year-old woman on amoxicillin and gentamicin for enterococcal IE has a creatinine that has doubled since treatment began.
items.explanation: Gentamicin dosing must follow levels and renal function: check the pre-dose level (target ≤1 mg/L, post-dose 3–5 mg/L) and adjust the dose.

items.stem: A 78-year-old man with a permanent pacemaker has persistent coagulase-negative staphylococcal bacteraemia. TOE shows a vegetation on the right ventricular lead.
items.explanation: Infected intracardiac hardware must be **removed**, as well as treated with prolonged antibiotics; the infection cannot be cleared otherwise.

questions.stem: A 74-year-old man with a bioprosthetic mitral valve has had 3 weeks of fever. Three blood culture sets grow Enterococcus faecalis. TTE shows no vegetation.
questions.leadIn: What is the most appropriate next investigation?
questions.explanation: A **negative TTE does not exclude IE**. With a **prosthetic valve** and a typical organism, **TOE** is the test of choice (>90% sensitive, best for prosthetic valves and abscesses).
whyNot: Waiting 6 weeks delays diagnosis; TTE is insensitive with prostheses.
A CXR cannot show vegetations.
Exercise testing has no role in IE.
Coronary angiography does not image vegetations.

ospe.identify: Splinter haemorrhages: thin dark linear streaks under the nail plate, a vasculitic/embolic stigma of IE.
Janeway lesions: painless flat haemorrhagic macules on the palm or sole (septic emboli). Contrast with tender Osler's nodes on the finger pulps.
Roth spot: a retinal haemorrhage with a pale centre seen on fundoscopy, an immune-vasculitic sign of IE.
IE signs map: nail-fold infarcts, conjunctival haemorrhages, petechiae and splinters. The commonest finding is a new or changing murmur (~90%).
Echo: a large vegetation on the tricuspid valve in a drug injector, i.e. right-sided (usually Staph. aureus) IE.
CT chest: multiple peripheral cavitating nodules = septic pulmonary emboli from tricuspid valve IE (presents with haemoptysis).
